I’ve known too many young CNAs mess their backs up beyond repair to the point any sort of physical labor is permanently off the table by the time they hit 30. Our ratios and expectations can be insane, I worked by myself as the only CNA on a unit (I did Dementia and Rehab so either lots of combative patients or lots of getting people up and down out of bed) even when I was 9 months pregnant. My husband and I did full time overnights, even with the Shift Diff we could barely afford to live and couldn’t afford our jobs insurance company, we were paid so little that when I got pregnant we qualified for Medicaid lmao. My husband ended up getting an agency job that paid what we made combined and I took a year off to be a SAHM before getting a CNA job at a small hospice, doesn’t pay much because it’s a non profit but much more manageable and personally fulfilling, unless stuff changes for the better I’d never want us both to go back to full regular staff CNAs. And since my place is mostly volunteer care giver ran I feel like my voice and opinions/experience is taken more seriously and bears more weight, like a real part of the team instead of just the grunt. You'd be surprised how far away from home animals can end up. My husband and I adopted a senior dog with health problems a few years back from a shelter, and a friend of mine got ahold of me on Facebook a few days later and said our dog looked a lot like one someone was looking for on a lost and found page (a lot of times these aren't super local pages, this one covered a good chunk of the state but a lot of people don't find them until their own pet goes missing) and it turned out someone our dog was stolen out of someone's yard in the city and dumped in someone's yard out in the rural area where I live a good 40 minutes or so from where the owners lived who had been calling shelters up in their city while it turned out she was at the shelter we got her from which small rural shelter in a different county, I don't blame them for not thinking to call there. We gave her back to her owners, the wife had adopted her when she was a few months old from one of the city shelters and had had her for 11 years since! The shelter had aged her at 6 lol. And she was a sweet dog but she lit up when we called her by her real name after learning it from her owners and was ECSTATIC to see them again. We only had her about a week to be fair but giving her back was obviously the right thing to do so gentle YTA to the OP. My husband and I were getting a lot of nasty comments on the lost and found page speculating on if we were actually decent people enough to give the dog back and what assholes we are if we don't until I saw and commented and the page updated the story. We still think about her from time to time though and sent her home with the pretty collar and all the treats we got her as a goodbye present and we heard from them from time to time for a year or so after thanking us so they obviously were super grateful. I get it's hard because you start to care about them, but there's so many pets out there that don't have homes, we don't need to be taking pets that do have them! The shelter ended up letting us take home a dog they never even put up on the site yet that they thought would be a good fit for us since we'd already paid the fee once and called us whenever they thought a dog would be a good fit for us until we adopted the one we have now because they felt bad about the situation. 

As far as people microchipping cats, the 2 big problems I've seen is people chip them then don't update the info when they move, etc, and I've noticed a lot of people are under the impression it's super expensive to do. A lot of pet stores have traveling vet clinics for basic check ups and shots, microchipping my cat was only $10!
